docs.title: A Scalable, Harmonized, and Cloud-friendly Ecosystem
docs.text:
Spatial transcriptomics (ST) technologies have revolutionized our ability to map molecular features with remarkable resolution—down to cellular and subcellular levels. The rapid development of sequencing-based platforms (e.g., Seq-Scope, Stereo-seq, Pixel-seq, 10x Visium HD) and imaging-based platforms (e.g., 10x Xenium, Vizgen MERSCOPE, CosMx SMI) has led to an explosion in the production of ST datasets across diverse tissues and species.

However, the rapid diversification of spatial transcriptomics platforms has led to heterogeneous data formats, inconsistent metadata schemas, and platform-specific analysis pipelines. Moreover, existing tools often lack the scalability to visualize gigapixel-scale data without downsampling.

To address this challenge, we introduce a scalable, harmonized, and cloud-friendly CartoScope ecosystem for spatial omics data across platforms.

docs.title: Ecosystem Overview
docs.text:
The CartoScope ecosystem is structured as illustrated below:

Together, they provide a unified solution for working with raw pixel-level spatial omics data — whether from our repository or your own lab — without sacrificing resolution or reproducibility.

docs.title: Core Module Details
docs.text:
CartLoaderCartoStoreCartoScope

CartLoader is the backend pipeline that prepares data for CartoScope. It provides a modular, reproducible tool to harmonize, integrate, analyze, and visualize raw high-resolution ST data across platforms.

Start here: one command per sample

run_together takes a sample from raw platform output to deployable CartoScope assets in a single command. To try it with no installation, run the prebuilt Docker image on the bundled starter dataset:

docker run --rm -v $(pwd)/out:/out hyunminkang/cartloader:latest \
  run_together --platform seqscope \
    --in-transcript /app/data/sge/transcripts.unsorted.tsv.gz \
    --out-dir /out/seqscope_hippo --id seqscope_hippo --width 18 --n-factor 6,12

Then continue with Get Started.

Table of Contents

The current document includes:

  • Get Started: run the pipeline with Docker or a local installation.
  • Guides: run_together for single and multiple samples, and tutorials for each platform.
  • Step-by-step: run the individual commands yourself for full control.
  • Reference: every command and option (actions, inputs, outputs, and parameters).
  • FAQ: common questions and troubleshooting.

Key Features

  • One-Command Pipeline: run_together runs conversion, FICTURE, cell analyses, image import, packaging, and optional publishing and AI annotation as one resumable Makefile, for one sample or a joint multi-sample model.
  • Cross-Platform Format Conversion: Converts raw SGE data from diverse ST platforms (public or your own) into a unified format, enabling consistent downstream processing.
  • Spatial Factor Inference: Applies FICTURE to infer spatial factors directly from pixel-level data, capturing biological patterns without requiring cell segmentation.
  • Multi-Modal Alignment: Aligns and overlays histology images with SGE data so all layers share a common coordinate system for pixel-accurate comparisons.
  • Cloud-Friendly Outputs: Produces compact, geospatially-indexed data formats suitable for web visualization and cloud storage.
  • Batch Integration and Sample Stitching: Supports joint analysis and SGE stitching across samples or platforms to reveal shared or differential features across tissues.
  • Modular and Reproducible Workflow: Orchestrates all steps through a Makefile-based system to ensure scalability, transparency, and reproducibility.

CartoStore acts as the data repository, hosting datasets processed by CartLoader and making them accessible to CartoScope. Visit the CartoStore Repository to access public datasets.

Key Features

  • Ready-to-use Datasets: Access processed, high-resolution datasets featuring FICTURE analysis results, morphology images, and cell analysis results, ready for immediate interactive exploration.
  • Broad Coverage: Spans diverse species, tissues, and disease models for a wide range of research needs.
  • Growing Repository: Continuously updated with new datasets as they are processed and added.

CartoScope is the frontend web-based App of our ecosystem, which enables interactive, pixel-level exploration of spatial omics data without requiring programming expertise. Visit the CartoScope Documentation for more details

Flexible Data Exploration

  • Explore Public Atlas: Access our ready-to-use collection of high-resolution spatial datasets.
  • Bring Your Own Data: Load, visualize, and interactively analyze your own custom datasets using our system.

Key Features

  • Ultra-high-resolution data at scale: Seamless web exploration for submicron-resolution ST data with hundreds of millions of spatial pixels, tens of thousands of genes, and billions of transcripts.
  • Molecular-level Inference with FICTURE: Powered by the latest version of FICTURE analysis, it helps interpret the spatial factors while preserving spatial accuracy and complexity. This method breaks the barrier of histology-based segmentation bias.
  • Dynamic Multi-layer Exploration: Interactive multi-layer maps with aligned multimodal datasets—including morphology images, cell-level analysis, molecular inference, and spot summaries—enabling exploration with rich, end-to-end spatial context.
  • Seamless Integration with Morphology Images: Support for diverse morphology image formats (H&E, DAPI, fluorescence reporters), seamlessly integrated with omics data.
  • Interactive ROI Analysis: Interactively define regions of interest, extract spatial features, and run differential expression analysis.
  • Save & Share Workspace: One-click save for your workspace (layers, styling, ROIs) and instant sharing with collaborators via unique links.
  • Scale-Up Your Own Data: Fully supports custom datasets—upload your own processing results to visualize and analyze your specific samples with the same powerful tools used for public data.
  • Open Access: Upload, screen, and share datasets worldwide at no cost.

docs.title: Installation Guide
docs.text:
This page installs CartLoader on your own machine.

No installation needed with Docker

The prebuilt image hyunminkang/cartloader:latest contains CartLoader and every tool it uses. If you only want to run the pipeline, see Quick Start with Docker instead.

In short:

  1. Create an environment for the non-Python tools (Section 2).
  2. Install CartLoader and its Python dependencies from the repository with uv or pip (Section 3).
  3. Build the bundled tools with build.sh (Section 4).
  4. Verify (Section 5).

docs.title: 1. Dependencies
docs.text: Instructions for installing everything below are in Sections 2, 3 and 4.

docs.title: 1.1 Required System Utilities
docs.text:
Confirm that these command-line programs are installed:

  • make, gzip, pigz, sort, bc, perl
  • bgzip, tabix (from htslib)

docs.title: 1.2 Build Tools
docs.text:
build.sh (Section 4) compiles several tools from source, which needs:

  • A C/C++ compiler, cmake, autoconf, automake, libtool, pkg-config, git
  • Development headers for zlib, bzip2, liblzma, libcurl, openssl, libpng, libdeflate, TBB and OpenCV

On Ubuntu/Debian, the Dockerfile lists the exact apt packages. On macOS, install them with Homebrew.

docs.title: 1.3 External Tools and Utilities
docs.text:
Python & Related Tooling

  • python 3.10 or newer (verified with versions 3.10 and 3.13)
  • uv (optional, recommended): a fast drop-in for pip

The Python packages CartLoader needs, including parquet-tools, are declared in its pyproject.toml and installed automatically in Section 3.

R & Related Packages

  • R from CRAN (verified with version 4.5.1). The R packages are installed in Section 3.2.

Tools Built from the Repository (git submodules, built by build.sh)

  • punkst: the latest, more efficient implementation of FICTURE
  • spatula
  • pmpoint
  • tippecanoe
  • go-pmtiles and geotiff2pmtiles: prebuilt binaries that build.sh downloads

Other Tools

  • ImageMagick: convert (ImageMagick 6) or magick (ImageMagick 7); spatula uses it for image I/O
  • gdal
  • aws-cli, only for uploading to S3

docs.title: 2. Setting Up the Environment using conda
docs.text:
We recommend isolating the project in a conda environment to avoid dependency conflicts. conda provides the Python interpreter and the non-Python tools (gdal, R, ...); the Python packages are installed from pyproject.toml in Section 3.

Without conda

If gdal, R and the other tools in Section 1 already come from your system (e.g. apt, Homebrew, or environment modules), you can skip this section and use a plain virtual environment instead; see Section 3.3.

docs.title: 2.1 Installing conda
docs.text:
If conda is not already available, download and install Miniconda or Anaconda.

Example installation of Miniconda3 on Linux:

env_dir=/path/to/your/directory/hosting/tools/      ## replace with your preferred tools directory
cd $env_dir

wget https://repo.anaconda.com/miniconda/Miniconda3-latest-Linux-x86_64.sh
bash Miniconda3-latest-Linux-x86_64.sh

docs.title: 2.2 Creating an Environment
docs.text:
Set up a fresh environment for CartLoader:

ENV_NAME="cart_env"   # define your environment name
PY_VERSION="3.13"     # define your python version (3.10 or newer)

conda create -n ${ENV_NAME} python=${PY_VERSION}
conda activate ${ENV_NAME}

docs.title: 2.3 Install Core Dependencies
docs.text:
Install the non-Python dependencies once the environment is active:

conda install -c conda-forge gdal aws-cli imagemagick pigz r-base

Install only these tools with conda. Leave the Python packages (including parquet-tools) to uv or pip in the next section: having the same Python package installed by both conda and pip is a common source of conflicts.

docs.title: 2.4 Installing uv (optional)
docs.text:
uv installs Python packages much faster than pip and uses the same commands (uv pip install ...). Skip this step to use pip.

curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh    # or: pip install uv

docs.title: 3.1 Installing the Python Package
docs.text:
Clone the repository, including its submodules, and install CartLoader with its Python dependencies. Run the install inside the activated environment from Section 2:

cd $env_dir
git clone --recursive https://github.com/seqscope/cartloader.git   # --recursive also fetches the submodules (Section 4)
cd cartloader
uvpip 
# uv installs into the active conda environment (it detects $CONDA_PREFIX)
uv pip install -e .

# or, with the optional AI annotation packages (see below):
uv pip install -e ".[ai]"

python -m pip install -e .

# or, with the optional AI annotation packages (see below):
python -m pip install -e ".[ai]"

The optional [ai] extra adds the packages for AI annotation of factors and cell clusters: run_together --anno / --anno-deep, anno_cartload_folder, and the annotate_* commands. Those commands also need the API key of the provider they call, set as an environment variable (ANTHROPIC_API_KEY, GEMINI_API_KEY, OPENAI_API_KEY or UMGPT_API_KEY).

Why an editable install (-e)

CartLoader reads its assets/ and the submodule binaries from the repository checkout, so it must be installed in editable mode, pointing at the checkout, rather than as a regular package. A git pull then updates the code without reinstalling; re-run the install command when the dependencies in pyproject.toml change (see Section 6).

docs.title: 3.2 Installing R Packages
docs.text: Rscript ./installation/install_r_packages.R

docs.title: 3.3 Alternative: a Virtual Environment without conda
docs.text:
If the non-Python tools come from your system instead of conda, create a virtual environment in the checkout and install into it:

uvpip 
cd $env_dir/cartloader
uv venv --python 3.13          # creates .venv; uv downloads that Python if it is missing
source .venv/bin/activate
uv pip install -e ".[ai]"      # or: uv pip install -e .

cd $env_dir/cartloader
python3 -m venv .venv          # python3 must be 3.10 or newer
source .venv/bin/activate
python -m pip install -e ".[ai]"   # or: python -m pip install -e .

Then install the R packages as in Section 3.2.

docs.title: 4. Initializing and Building Submodules
docs.text:
The --recursive clone in Section 3 already fetched the submodules. For a checkout cloned without it, fetch them now:

cd $env_dir/cartloader
git submodule update --init --recursive

Then build the bundled tools with build.sh, the same step the Docker image uses:

cd $env_dir/cartloader/submodules
bash build.sh

It builds htslib, qgenlib, spatula, pmpoint, tippecanoe and punkst, and downloads the pmtiles and geotiff2pmtiles binaries. ImageMagick is not built; install it with conda (Section 2.3) or see Section 4.5.

The tools must stay inside submodules/

CartLoader commands, and run_together in particular, look for these tools at fixed locations inside the checkout (for example submodules/punkst/bin/punkst and submodules/pmtiles/pmtiles), not on your PATH. Build them in place as below; a copy installed elsewhere is not found.

If a step of build.sh fails, rebuild that tool on its own as follows, then rerun build.sh or continue with the remaining tools.

docs.title: 4.1 Installing spatula
docs.text:
cd ${env_dir}/cartloader/submodules/spatula
mkdir -p build && cd build
cmake ..
make -j 4

build.sh builds htslib and qgenlib first, which spatula and pmpoint link against; build them first if you start from a clean checkout.

docs.title: 4.2 Installing punkst
docs.text:
punkst provides FICTURE (Si et al., Nature Methods 2024). Build it inside the submodule so that submodules/punkst/bin/punkst exists:

cd ${env_dir}/cartloader/submodules/punkst
mkdir -p build && cd build
cmake ..
make -j 4

For build prerequisites and troubleshooting, see the punkst installation guide.

Question

  • What is FICTURE and punkst?

docs.title: 4.3 Installing tippecanoe
docs.text:
cd ${env_dir}/cartloader/submodules/tippecanoe
make -j 4

CartLoader uses the binary built in place (submodules/tippecanoe/tippecanoe); make install is not needed.

docs.title: 4.4 Installing go-pmtiles and geotiff2pmtiles
docs.text:
Both are downloaded as prebuilt binaries for your OS and architecture:

cd ${env_dir}/cartloader/submodules
bash install-pmtiles.sh --dest ./pmtiles
bash install-geotiff2pmtiles.sh --dest ./geotiff2pmtiles

docs.title: 4.5 Installing ImageMagick
docs.text:
Skip this step if ImageMagick was already installed via conda in Section 2.3 or by your system's package manager.

cd ${env_dir}/cartloader/submodules/ImageMagick
./configure     # Alternatively, run `./configure --prefix=${env_dir}/cartloader/submodules/ImageMagick`.
make
make install

docs.title: 5. Verifying the Installation
docs.text:
Run the following commands to verify CartLoader and its dependencies:

# activate your environment if you did not
conda activate ${ENV_NAME}       # or, for Section 3.3: source .venv/bin/activate

# verify the installation of cartloader: lists the available commands
cartloader

# check the system tools, Python packages and R packages
python ./installation/check_dependencies.py

# check that the bundled tools were built
ls -l submodules/punkst/bin/punkst submodules/spatula/bin/spatula submodules/pmpoint/bin/pmpoint \
      submodules/tippecanoe/tippecanoe submodules/pmtiles/pmtiles submodules/geotiff2pmtiles/geotiff2pmtiles

check_dependencies.py reads the Python dependencies from pyproject.toml. Packages of the optional [ai] extra are reported as optional and do not fail the check.

Then try the local quick start.

docs.title: 6. Updating CartLoader
docs.text:
cd $env_dir/cartloader
git pull
git submodule update --init --recursive

# pick up any dependency changes in pyproject.toml (include [ai] if you installed it)
uv pip install -e ".[ai]"          # or: python -m pip install -e ".[ai]"

# rebuild the bundled tools for the updated submodule versions
cd submodules && bash build.sh

Both steps matter after each update: new code may need a Python package added to pyproject.toml (a stale environment fails with an error such as requires the 'imagecodecs' package), and the pipeline passes options that only the tool versions pinned by the repository understand (an outdated build fails with an "unknown option" error or a usage message).

docs.title: Why did my AWS upload fail, and how can I fix it?
docs.text: If cartloader upload_aws fails, it is usually one of the issues below.

docs.title: 1) AWS credentials are missing or invalid
docs.text:
Common messages:

  • Unable to locate credentials
  • The security token included in the request is invalid
  • ExpiredToken

Checks:

aws sts get-caller-identity
aws configure list

Fix:

  • Configure credentials (aws configure) or set AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID, AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY, and (if needed) AWS_SESSION_TOKEN.
  • If you use temporary credentials, refresh them before running upload.

docs.title: 2) Permission denied on bucket/prefix
docs.text:
Common messages:

  • AccessDenied
  • An error occurred (AccessDenied) when calling ...

Checks:

aws s3 ls s3://your-bucket/
aws s3 ls s3://your-bucket/your-prefix/

Fix:

  • Ensure IAM policy allows at least s3:ListBucket, s3:PutObject, and s3:GetObject on the target bucket/prefix.
  • Confirm bucket policy does not block your principal.

docs.title: 3) Wrong S3 destination path
docs.text:
Common issue:

  • Upload appears to "succeed" but files are not where you expected.

Fix:

  • Verify --s3-dir is a full S3 URI like s3://bucket/path.
  • In collection mode (--in-list), remember each sample is uploaded to a subdirectory under --s3-dir.

docs.title: 4) Input directory/catalog problems
docs.text:
Common messages:

  • Missing catalog.yaml
  • Missing expected PMTiles/assets

Fix:

  • Confirm --in-dir points to a completed run_cartload2 (or collection parent for run_cartload2_multi).
  • In single mode, verify catalog.yaml exists (or pass --catalog-yaml explicitly).

docs.title: 5) Docker run cannot see AWS credentials
docs.text:
If local aws works but Docker upload fails, credentials may not be available inside the container.

Fix:

  • Mount/pass AWS credentials into the container (for example, ~/.aws) or pass required AWS_* env vars.
  • Confirm the aws binary inside container is available (or set --aws).

docs.title: 6) Region, endpoint, or network issues
docs.text:
Common messages:

  • Could not connect to the endpoint URL
  • timeout/name resolution errors

Fix:

  • Verify internet/VPN/proxy settings.
  • Check bucket region and AWS CLI region configuration.

docs.title: Minimal preflight before upload
docs.text:
aws sts get-caller-identity
aws s3 ls s3://your-bucket/

If both pass, retry:

cartloader upload_aws --in-dir /path/to/cartload2 --s3-dir s3://your-bucket/your-prefix

See also:

  • AWS upload reference

docs.title: How do I decide orientation for background image import?
docs.text:
Use the SGE visualization from sge_convert as your orientation reference. Compare your raw background image against it to determine whether the image needs rotation and/or flips before it is imported.

Use the north-up reference

sge_convert --sge-visual --north-up writes xy_northup.tif (next to xy.png), the SGE rendered in the north-up view that CartoScope displays. Compare against xy_northup.tif, not xy.png.

docs.title: Recommended workflow
docs.text:
1. Generate SGE reference image:
  2. Run sge_convert with --sge-visual --north-up.
  3. Locate xy_northup.tif in the SGE output directory.
  4. Open your background image and xy_northup.tif side by side.
  5. Match major landmarks (tissue outline, empty corners, distinctive structures).
  6. Infer the transform:
  7. Rotation: --rotate 90, --rotate 180, or --rotate 270
  8. Flips: --flip-horizontal and/or --flip-vertical
  9. Run a quick trial import and verify overlap in the viewer.
  10. If needed, adjust transform and rerun.

docs.title: Applying the transform
docs.text:
• import_image: --rotate 90|180|270, --flip-horizontal, --flip-vertical.
  • run_together: the same transform as the rotate, flip_horizontal, and flip_vertical keys of the image's entry (--image, the --images sheet, or the config). See Image Modalities for which image kinds honor them.

docs.title: Practical tips
docs.text:
• Start with rotation only; add flips only if left/right or up/down are mirrored.
  • Rotation is applied before flips.
  • Keep one transform per image source and reuse it for consistency.

See also:

  • Background Image Import reference
  • SGE Format Conversion reference

docs.title: Which interface should I use to run the pipeline?
docs.text:
Use run_together. It is the recommended interface: one command runs the whole pipeline (SGE conversion → FICTURE → cell analyses → images → packaging → optional publishing) for any supported platform, for one sample or many, as a single resumable Makefile.

The individual commands remain available when you need control that run_together does not expose.

Interface What it is Best for run_together (recommended) One command for the whole pipeline, with per-platform defaults, sample sheets, and a JSON config for full control Almost every run: single samples, cohorts with a joint model, batches of independent samples Individual commands Call sge_convert, run_ficture2, run_cartload2, import_*, upload_* yourself Custom pipelines, a parameter run_together does not expose, debugging one stage, tight HPC integration run_xenium / run_visiumhd (legacy) Older per-platform orchestrators Existing scripts only; see Legacy Orchestrators

docs.title: Quick decision rule
docs.text:
• Running a supported platform, one sample or many? → run_together. Start with Get Started, then the single-sample or multi-sample guide.
  • A platform without a built-in profile, or a custom format? → still run_together, with --platform generic (see the Generic platform page); drop to the individual commands only if that is not enough.
  • Need to customize or debug one stage? → the individual commands, introduced in Step-by-step.

They interoperate

run_together calls the same commands and produces the same catalog.yaml + PMTiles. You can prototype with run_together, then rerun a single stage by hand.

See also: Run with Docker or locally? · Which platform tutorial?

docs.title: How do I choose the right tutorial for my platform?
docs.text:
There is a platform tutorial for each of these platforms: 10x Xenium, Vizgen MERSCOPE, CosMx SMI, 10x Visium HD, Stereo-seq, Seq-Scope, and Pixel-seq, plus a Generic tutorial for any other platform's transcript table. Each starts from a small dataset, shows the single run_together command, and then walks through the individual commands.

For your own data, see the platform's page under Platforms: it lists the exact files run_together looks for and example commands. Built-in profiles exist for 10x Xenium, 10x Visium HD, CosMx SMI, MERSCOPE (MERFISH), Illumina, Stereo-seq, and Seq-Scope, plus a generic profile for anything else.

If your platform is not listed above, see:

  • My platform is not in the supported list. Can I still use CartLoader?

docs.title: I am not sure whether to run with Docker or run locally. Which one should I choose?
docs.text:
Use this quick comparison to choose a run mode.

Mode Good Bad Best for Docker run Fastest setup; reproducible environment; fewer dependency/version issues; easier onboarding for new users Docker install required; container startup overhead; file mounts/permissions can be confusing; less convenient for editing internals First-time users, tutorials, shared team workflows, reproducible reruns Local run Direct access to local files/tools; easier debugging and profiling; no container boundary; easier to customize and extend More setup effort; dependency conflicts are more likely; environments can drift across machines Power users, developers, custom pipelines, tight integration with local tooling/HPC modules

docs.title: Quick decision rule
docs.text:
• Choose Docker if your priority is getting started quickly and reproducibly.

  • Choose local if your priority is deep customization, debugging, or development.

  • Docker guide: Run with Docker

  • Local guide: Run Locally

Choosing an interface (not a run mode)

This page is about where to run (Docker vs local). For which command to drive the pipeline — run_together vs run_xenium/run_visiumhd vs individual modules — see Which interface should I use?.

docs.title: How do I define scaling (--units-per-um)?
docs.text:
--units-per-um means: how many coordinate units in your input equal 1 micrometer (um).

In other words:

units_per_um = input_coordinate_units / um

docs.title: Quick rules
docs.text:
• If input coordinates are already in um: use --units-per-um 1.
  • If input coordinates are in pixels: use --units-per-um = pixels_per_um = 1 / microns_per_pixel.
  • If input coordinates are in nanometers (nm): use --units-per-um 1000.

docs.title: Where to set it
docs.text:
• run_together: --units-per-um (or ingest.units_per_um in the config) is passed to SGE conversion. Most platform profiles already know their platform's unit, so you usually only set it for --platform generic or unusual inputs; your platform page says whether the profile fixes it.
  • sge_convert: --units-per-um, as in the examples below.

docs.title: Platform guidance
docs.text:
• 10x Visium HD: prefer --scale-json (from scalefactors_json.json) so scaling is computed automatically.
  • SeqScope (raw per-molecule TSV route): coordinates are in nanometers, so the default is 1000.
  • Illumina StrataMap: coordinates are embedded in the barcode, and two conventions exist — older barcodes are in nanometers (SBC:433503:2393851, --units-per-um 1000), current ones in microns (SBC:686.951:4668.15, --units-per-um 1). sge_convert reads the barcode file and picks the right one, printing what it used; pass --units-per-um to override it.
  • Other platforms / generic CSV: set --units-per-um based on your file's coordinate unit metadata.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Using 1 when coordinates are actually in pixels.
  • Mixing units across samples in one project.
  • Rounding scale too aggressively (keep enough precision).

docs.title: Sanity checks after conversion
docs.text:
• Tissue width/height should be in a realistic micrometer range for your assay.
  • Spot/transcript spacing should look plausible in generated visualization.
  • If geometry looks too small/large by a constant factor, re-check --units-per-um.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
# Coordinates already in um
cartloader sge_convert ... --units-per-um 1

# Coordinates in pixels, and microns_per_pixel = 0.2125
# units_per_um = 1 / 0.2125 = 4.705882...
cartloader sge_convert ... --units-per-um 4.705882

# Visium HD: use scale JSON instead of manual factor
cartloader sge_convert ... --scale-json /path/to/scalefactors_json.json

See also:

  • SGE Format Conversion reference

docs.title: FICTURE
docs.text:
FICTURE is a segmentation-free method. It reconstructs the fine-scale tissue structure by first decomposing gene expression patterns across the tissue section into spatial factors and then assigns each pixel to these factors using local context. Biologically, these inferred factors may correspond to specific cell types, functional or physiological states, subcellular domains, or extracellular transcriptomic signatures.

By default, FICTURE learns the spatial factors by implementing a standard latent Dirichlet allocation (LDA) model on a hexagonal grid overlay of the spatial coordinates. Optionally, spatial factors can also be derived from external sources, such as single-cell or single-nucleus RNA-seq reference datasets, or from spatially agnostic factor learning methods (e.g., Seurat, Scanpy).

docs.title: Punkst
docs.text:
To efficiently run FICTURE-based inference, CartLoader integrates punkst, an optimized implementation of FICTURE that maintains output equivalence while enhancing computational scalability and performance.

Currently, run_ficture2 uses the punkst version of FICTURE.

docs.title: Where are outputs written, and which files should I keep?
With run_together
docs.text:
Everything goes under --out-dir:

<out-dir>/
├── run_together.mk            # the generated Makefile
├── run_together.resolved.json # the fully resolved configuration (provenance)
├── mk/                        # per-stage done flags
├── tsv/<id>/                  # converted SGE
├── fic/                       # FICTURE models, decoding, and cell analyses
└── cartl/<dir>/               # catalog.yaml + PMTiles  ← the deployable result

The packaged directory <dir> is <out-dir name>-<id>, shortened to <id> when the two are equal. A joint multi-sample run writes one such directory per sample plus cartl/multi-catalog.yaml.

Keep cartl/ (that is what CartoScope reads; upload it as a unit) and run_together.resolved.json (it records exactly what was run). tsv/ and fic/ are needed to rerun or extend the analysis, e.g. to add a model with a different --n-factor without repeating SGE conversion; delete them only when you are done.

docs.title: With the individual commands
docs.text:
Each command writes into its own --out-dir, plus a manifest that records its key artifacts:

  • sge_convert: unified SGE files + sge_assets.json
  • run_ficture2: models and decoding outputs + ficture.params.json (run_ficture2_multi writes ficture.multi.params.json)
  • run_cartload2: PMTiles layers + catalog.yaml (and ficture_assets.json)

Keep the final manifests and catalog.yaml, the PMTiles they reference, and any SGE you plan to reuse. Remove later, if needed, intermediate files that the pipeline regenerates, and diagnostic plots or logs you no longer need. Before deleting, confirm your next step does not depend on those files.

docs.title: FAQ Overview
docs.text:
This section answers frequently asked questions about running CartLoader.

Contact Us

To report issues or ask questions, please submit your questions or report issues via:

  • GitHub Issues: seqscope/cartloader Issues
  • Email Support: cartoscope@umich.edu

How to submit an issue

When reporting an issue, it'd be very helpful to include:

  • Your OS/environment (Docker or local)
  • Exact command that failed
  • Full error message
  • A minimal reproducible input if possible

docs.title: Choosing How to Run
docs.text:
• Which interface should I use to run the pipeline?
  • I am not sure whether to run with Docker or run locally. Which one should I choose?
  • How do I choose the right tutorial for my platform?
  • My platform is not in the supported list. Can I still use CartLoader?

docs.title: cartloader Function Questions
docs.text:
• How do I define scaling (--units-per-um)?
  • What is FICTURE and punkst?
  • Why use Multi‑Sample FICTURE Analysis?
  • How do I decide orientation for background image import?
  • What are the Zenodo token and deposition ID, and how do you get them?
  • Why did my AWS upload fail, and how can I fix it?

docs.title: Execution Questions
docs.text:
• How do I resume a run, or rerun everything from scratch?
  • How can I speed up runs safely?
  • Where are outputs written, and which files should I keep?

docs.title: How do I resume a run, or rerun everything from scratch?
docs.text:
run_together and the individual CartLoader commands plan their work as a Makefile, so:

  • Resume: rerun the same command. Steps whose outputs already exist are skipped, so an interrupted or failed run continues from where it stopped.
  • Rerun everything: add --restart, which rebuilds every step (make -B).
  • Preview: add --dry-run to write the Makefile and print the planned commands without executing them.

docs.title: With run_together
docs.text:
# Resume after an interruption: the same command again
cartloader run_together --platform 10x_xenium --in-dir IN --out-dir OUT --id my_sample

# Run or skip particular stages (stages outside the selection are assumed done)
cartloader run_together ... --only ingest,ficture
cartloader run_together ... --skip images

# Rebuild everything
cartloader run_together ... --restart

Changing a setting such as --n-factor or --width adds new models alongside the existing ones on the next run. --restart is only needed to redo steps whose outputs already exist.

docs.title: With the individual commands
docs.text:
cartloader run_ficture2 ... --dry-run     # inspect commands only
cartloader run_ficture2 ... --restart     # force a full rerun

See also:

  • run_together reference
  • FICTURE Analysis reference

docs.title: How can I speed up runs safely?
docs.text:
The main controls, available in run_together and most individual commands:

  • -j / --n-jobs: number of parallel jobs (pipeline-level parallelism)
  • --threads: threads per job (tool-level parallelism)

The two multiply: -j 4 --threads 4 can keep about 16 cores busy.

docs.title: Tuning guide
docs.text:
• Start with -j × --threads close to the number of CPU cores.
  • Increase gradually while monitoring RAM and disk I/O.
  • If the machine becomes unstable (heavy swapping, stalled I/O), reduce -j first.
  • Use higher --threads when the work is dominated by a few compute-heavy steps (FICTURE training and decoding), and higher -j when there are many small steps (packaging many gene bins, many samples).

docs.title: Rules of thumb
docs.text:
• run_together on a multi-sample run: -j parallelizes across samples and stages; per-sample packaging in a joint run also uses -j.
  • Fewer gene bins (--bin-count) make packaging faster, at the cost of coarser grouping in the point layers.
  • Shared servers and HPC login nodes: be conservative and follow local policy.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
cartloader run_together --platform 10x_xenium --in-dir IN --out-dir OUT -j 4 --threads 4

See also:

  • run_together reference
  • Asset Packaging reference

docs.title: My platform is not in the supported list. Can I still use CartLoader?
docs.text: Yes. Any platform that can produce a transcript-level table works.

docs.title: 1. Prepare a transcript table
docs.text:
A transcript-level CSV/TSV with these fields:

  • X coordinate
  • Y coordinate
  • feature name (typically gene)
  • count (or one row per transcript)

docs.title: 2. Run run_together with the generic profile (recommended)
docs.text:
cartloader run_together \
  --platform generic \
  --raw-transcript /path/to/input.tsv.gz \
  --colname-transcript-x x \
  --colname-transcript-y y \
  --colname-transcript-feature gene \
  --colname-transcript-count count \
  --units-per-um 1 \
  --out-dir /path/to/out/my_sample \
  --width 18 --n-factor 12

The Generic tutorial walks through this on real data, including a comma-separated file and a cell-ID column. --raw-transcript sends the table through SGE conversion; the --colname-transcript-* options name its columns, and --units-per-um sets how many coordinate units make one micrometer. See the Generic platform page for every option, including a cell-ID column for cell analyses.

docs.title: Alternative: convert with sge_convert yourself
docs.text:
To control the conversion directly, run sge_convert in generic mode, then continue with the step-by-step commands (run_ficture2, run_cartload2, uploads):

cartloader sge_convert \
  --platform generic \
  --in-csv /path/to/input.tsv \
  --csv-delim $'\t' \
  --csv-colname-x x \
  --csv-colname-y y \
  --csv-colname-feature-name gene \
  --csv-colname-count count \
  --units-per-um 1 \
  --out-dir /path/to/out/sge

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• Start with a small subset first to validate formatting and scaling.
  • If your file has comments, delimiters, or headers that differ from defaults, set the corresponding options explicitly.

See also:

  • How do I define scaling (--units-per-um)?
  • SGE Format Conversion reference

docs.title: Why use Multi‑Sample FICTURE Analysis?
docs.text:
CartLoader supports analyzing ≥2 samples in three ways:

  • A joint run_together run (--samples): lists the samples in a sheet and trains one shared model across all of them, then packages each sample against it. This is the recommended way; internally it uses run_ficture2_multi.
  • Multi‑sample FICTURE analysis with the individual commands (run_ficture2_multi): the same joint model, run step by step.
  • SGE stitch + single‑sample analysis (sge_stitch → run_ficture2): stitch multiple SGEs into a single mosaic, then train one model on that mosaic.

For unrelated samples that should not share a model, use run_together --out-root instead: each sample gets its own independent model.

What to expect

  • Shared factors/comparability: a joint model learns a cohort‑wide latent basis and returns per‑sample decodes for direct comparison. The stitch approach yields a single model over the merged mosaic; useful when you need a unified coordinate system (e.g., tiling adjacent sections).
  • Efficiency and scale: a joint model fits once for the cohort and decodes per sample, avoiding repeated runs and post‑hoc alignment. Stitching can be simpler for mosaics but often increases I/O and memory due to very large merged files.

Recommendation

  • Prefer a joint run_together run (or run_ficture2_multi) for most cohorts: clean per‑sample outputs and better computational efficiency. Use stitching when a single shared coordinate frame is required.
  • If you choose stitching, plan for higher resource usage (RAM, disk, and I/O). Large mosaics can be slow to generate and train on, and may require substantially more memory and temporary storage than per‑sample runs.

docs.title: What are the Zenodo token and deposition ID, and how do you get them?
Zenodo Token File
docs.text:
CartLoader uses the Zenodo API for uploads. To authenticate, Zenodo requires an access token.

To obtain a token:

  1. Log in to Zenodo.
  2. Open Applications.
  3. Click "New Token" and select scopes such as deposit:write and deposit:actions.
  4. Copy the generated token.
  5. Save it in a plain text file and pass that file path to --zenodo-token.

docs.title: Zenodo Deposition ID
docs.text:
A deposition ID is the numeric identifier of a Zenodo deposition (dataset record). If you already created one, find it in the URL, for example:

https://zenodo.org/deposit/1234567
                            ^^^^^^^
                           deposition ID

See also:

  • Zenodo upload reference

docs.title: AI Annotation (anno_cartload_folder)
docs.text:
Usually run for you

run_together calls anno_cartload_folder in its anno stage: --anno uses the per-factor annotator and --anno-deep adds --deep. This page is for annotating a packaged directory directly, step by step.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
anno_cartload_folder AI-annotates every factor of a packaged CartoScope dataset. For each factor listed in the catalog it writes an alias TSV (<factor-id>-alias-ai.tsv, factor index → label) and records that file in the catalog under the alias_ai key. Two annotators are available:

  • Default: annotate_bulk_de_with_ai labels each factor from its DE table, one LLM call per factor.
  • --deep: annotate_factors_with_llm labels all factors of a model together in one deep-reasoning call, with alternative interpretations, and also writes an annotation table and an interactive HTML report.

It operates on a local --cartl-dir or an already-uploaded --s3-dir (download, annotate, upload back).

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• A packaged directory with a catalog.yaml (from run_cartload2) or, for --multi-sample, a run_cartload2_multi output root with multi-catalog.yaml.
  • An API key for the chosen --api-type in the environment: ANTHROPIC_API_KEY (claude), OPENAI_API_KEY (openai), GEMINI_API_KEY (google), or UMGPT_API_KEY (umgpt).
  • For --s3-dir: the boto3 package and AWS credentials.

docs.title: Modes
docs.text:
Single sample (default)Multi-sample (--multi-sample)Deep annotation (--deep)S3 in-place (--s3-dir)

Annotates one packaged directory, reading assets.factors from its catalog.yaml.

cartloader anno_cartload_folder \
  --cartl-dir cartl/mydataset \
  --tissue "Kidney" --organism human

Annotates the shared factors of a joint run once at the cartl/ root (from the multi-catalog.yaml written by run_cartload2_multi), then copies each shared alias TSV into every sample sub-folder listed under samples: and records it in that sample's catalog.yaml. A sample-specific factor without a shared annotation is annotated in its own folder.

cartloader anno_cartload_folder \
  --cartl-dir cartl \
  --multi-sample \
  --tissue "Kidney" --organism human

Factor IDs are hyphenated (t12_f48 → t12-f48) in alias file names, so a shared alias matches the per-sample factor id in each <multi_id>-<sample_id>/catalog.yaml.

Runs annotate_factors_with_llm per factor model. In a multi-sample root, per-sample tissues can come from a sample sheet (id and tissue columns), which may replace --tissue.

cartloader anno_cartload_folder \
  --cartl-dir cartl \
  --multi-sample --deep \
  --sample-sheet samples.tsv \
  --organism human --api-type claude --effort high

Downloads the catalog and the files needed for annotation, annotates them in a local temporary directory, and uploads the alias TSVs and the updated catalog back to S3. Downloads use the default boto3 credentials; uploads use --profile. --multi-sample has no effect in this mode.

cartloader anno_cartload_folder \
  --s3-dir s3://cartostore/data/batch=2026_07/mycollection/mydataset \
  --tissue "Kidney" --organism human --profile cartostore

docs.title: Skipping and reusing annotations
docs.text:
• Factors that already carry an alias or alias_ai key (--yaml-key-skip) are skipped, so reruns only annotate new factors. Factors without a de entry are skipped, except in --deep mode when they have a model (model or post) entry.
  • Pass --reuse-results-from <dir> to copy alias TSVs from <dir> instead of calling the AI, e.g., to propagate one hand-checked sample to a cohort. In --multi-sample mode it applies only to the shared (root) pass; the sample propagation always reuses the shared results just written.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
Input (choose one):

  • --cartl-dir (str): Local packaged directory.
  • --s3-dir (str): s3://… prefix of an uploaded dataset.

Annotation context:

  • --organism (str, required): Organism/species.
  • --tissue (str): Tissue name. Required, except with --deep --multi-sample when --sample-sheet gives samples a tissue (samples without one fall back to --tissue).

Annotator:

  • --api-type (str): claude, openai, google, or umgpt (default: claude).
  • --model (str): LLM model name (default: claude-opus-4-8; with --deep, the annotate_factors_with_llm default for the API type, e.g. claude-opus-5-5 for claude).
  • --threads (int): Annotation threads (default: 1).
  • --deep (flag): Use annotate_factors_with_llm instead of annotate_bulk_de_with_ai.
  • --effort (str): --deep reasoning effort: low, medium, high, xhigh, or max (default: high).
  • --sample-sheet (str): --deep with --multi-sample: TSV with id and tissue columns (blank, -, ., or NA mean unset).

Multi-sample and reuse:

  • --multi-sample (flag): Treat --cartl-dir as a joint-run root; annotate multi-catalog.yaml and propagate.
  • --multi-catalog (str): Multi-catalog file name (default: multi-catalog.yaml).
  • --catalog (str): Per-sample catalog file name (default: catalog.yaml).
  • --reuse-results-from (str): Copy alias TSVs from this directory instead of annotating.

Alias and catalog keys:

  • --alias-suffix (str): Alias file suffix (default: -alias-ai.tsv).
  • --backup-suffix (str): Suffix of the pre-update catalog copy (default: .bak).
  • --yaml-key-store (str): Factor key that records the alias file (default: alias_ai).
  • --yaml-key-skip (list of str): Factor keys that mark an annotated factor (default: alias alias_ai).

S3 (with --s3-dir):

  • --profile (str): AWS profile for uploading results (default: default).
  • --skip-upload (flag): Annotate locally only; do not upload back.
  • --tmp-dir (str): Download and staging directory (default: a directory named after the last component of --s3-dir, under the current directory).

docs.title: Output
docs.text:
In each annotated directory:

  • <factor-id>-alias-ai.tsv: Alias TSV (index, alias) for every annotated factor.
  • With --deep, next to it: <factor-id>-alias-ai.annotations.tsv (per-factor label, confidence, alternatives, evidence), <factor-id>-alias-ai.html (report), and <factor-id>-alias-ai.llm/ (saved LLM requests and responses).
  • The catalog rewritten in place with alias_ai: <factor-id>-alias-ai.tsv on each annotated factor, plus a backup of the previous catalog at <catalog><backup-suffix> (written on every run).

For --multi-sample, alias files are written at the cartl/ root and in every sample sub-folder listed under samples: in multi-catalog.yaml.

docs.title: Annotate Factors with an LLM (annotate_factors_with_llm)
docs.text:
Usually run for you

run_together --anno-deep runs this command through anno_cartload_folder --deep, once per factor model, and records the result in the catalog. This page is for running the annotator directly, step by step.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
annotate_factors_with_llm labels the latent factors of a cartloader run (cell types or transcriptional programs) with a generative LLM that sees all factors at once, so it can contrast factors and answer Unresolved when the evidence is weak. For each factor it returns a best-guess label, kind (cell type or program), compartment, confidence, key genes, rationale, and alternative interpretations when the markers support more than one reading. It writes an alias TSV in the same format as annotate_bulk_de_with_ai (a drop-in for the catalog's alias_ai key), a per-factor annotation table, and a self-contained interactive HTML report.

Evidence per factor:

  • marker genes: the top --top-n genes by chi-square and by fold enrichment, interleaved;
  • abundance (share of counts), DE support (number of enriched genes), and per-gene specificity (needs the model matrix);
  • multi-sample: which samples and tissues hold the factor, and its top genes within each sample.

All factors are sent in one call by default; a call whose answer exceeds the output budget is split in halves automatically.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Packaged factor files, addressed by a prefix (see Inputs): a model matrix (-model.tsv) and/or a DE table (-bulk-de.tsv or -de.tsv; computed from the model when absent).
  • An API key in the environment for --api-type: ANTHROPIC_API_KEY (or ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN) for claude, OPENAI_API_KEY for openai, GEMINI_API_KEY for google, UMGPT_API_KEY for umgpt. Not needed with --dry-run or --report-only.
  • For --api-type claude: the anthropic Python package, version 0.77.0 or later.

docs.title: Inputs
docs.text:
Point --prefix at a factor prefix of a packaged directory:

Run Example prefix Files read Single sample cartl/<sample>/t18-f192 <prefix>-bulk-de.tsv, <prefix>-model.tsv Multi-sample root cartl/t12-f192 <prefix>-de.tsv, <prefix>-model.tsv, and each sample's <multi_id>-<sample>/t12-f192-pixel-pseudobulk.tsv.gz

<prefix>-rgb.tsv, when present, gives each factor its CartoScope color in the report. For the factor model, -model.tsv, -model.tsv.gz, or -pseudobulk.tsv.gz is used, whichever exists first.

Samples of a multi-sample run are found through multi-catalog.yaml next to the prefix or, without it, from sibling sub-directories holding a pseudobulk for the prefix. A run with a single sample is annotated as single-sample. The tissue of every sample is --tissue, or the tissue column of --sample-sheet (e.g., the run_together sample sheet, matched by id) for pan-tissue runs. A single-sample dataset requires --tissue.

docs.title: Example Usage
docs.text:
# Single sample
cartloader annotate_factors_with_llm \
  --prefix cartl/sample-rep1/t18-f192 \
  --organism mouse --tissue "whole mouse pup" \
  --api-type claude

# Multi-sample root with per-sample tissues
cartloader annotate_factors_with_llm \
  --prefix cartl/t12-f192 \
  --organism human --sample-sheet samples.tsv \
  --api-type claude

# Preview the prompts and an evidence-only report without calling the LLM
cartloader annotate_factors_with_llm \
  --prefix cartl/sample-rep1/t18-f192 \
  --organism mouse --tissue "whole mouse pup" \
  --api-type claude --dry-run

docs.title: Candidate labels
docs.text:
Candidate labels are optional suggestions sent with the prompt (or a closed list with --closed).

  • --candidates auto generates one list per tissue with the same provider (reasoning effort --candidate-effort, default low), caches it under --candidate-cache-dir, and saves the merged list as <stem>.candidates.json. Uncached lists are generated with an LLM call even under --dry-run; --report-only reuses the saved <stem>.candidates.json.
  • --candidates FILE [FILE ...] uses JSON lists made by generate_candidate_labels_with_llm; multiple files are merged by label.

generate_candidate_labels_with_llm makes one LLM call per tissue context (no marker genes are sent), so a list can be reused for every dataset from that tissue:

cartloader generate_candidate_labels_with_llm \
  --organism human --tissue "lung cancer" "lymph node" \
  --api-type claude --out candidates.json

Its options: --organism, --tissue (one or more), --out, --api-type (all required); --mode (default either), --cache-dir (default ./jevanno_cache), --no-generate (use cached lists only), --min-candidates / --max-candidates (default 80 / 200), --model-name, --effort (default low), --max-output-tokens (default 64000), --threads (default 8), plus --no-fallbacks, --api-base-url, --request-timeout, --verbose. Lists are cached per model and effort, and a cached list made at the same or higher effort is reused.

docs.title: Input/Output Parameters
docs.text:
• --prefix (str): Factor prefix (see Inputs).
  • --model (str): Factor model matrix TSV, gene × factor (default: from --prefix).
  • --de (str): Bulk DE TSV (default: from --prefix; computed from the model when absent).
  • --rgb (str): Factor color table (default: <prefix>-rgb.tsv if present).
  • --out (str): Output alias TSV (default: <prefix>-alias-ai.tsv); companion files share its stem. Required without --prefix.
  • --organism (str, required): e.g., human, mouse.
  • --tissue (str): Tissue context for all samples (unless the sample sheet gives one per sample).
  • --sample-sheet (alias --samples) (str): Multi-sample TSV with id and optional tissue (and pseudobulk) columns.
  • --candidates (list of str): Candidate label JSON file(s), or auto.
  • --api-type (str, required): claude, openai, umgpt, or google.
Auxiliary Parameters

Annotation:

  • --mode (str): cell_type, program, or either (default: either).
  • --closed (flag): Restrict labels to the candidates (requires --candidates).
  • --single-sample (flag): Treat the prefix as single-sample even if sample directories are found (cannot be combined with --sample-sheet).
  • --multi-catalog (str): Multi-sample catalog next to the prefix (default: multi-catalog.yaml).
  • --candidate-cache-dir (str): Cache for --candidates auto (default: ~/.cache/cartloader/llm_candidates).
  • --candidate-effort (str): Effort for --candidates auto (default: low).

Evidence:

  • --primary-rank / --secondary-rank (str): DE ranking columns (default: Chi2 / FoldChange).
  • --top-n (int): Top genes per ranking column (default: 10).
  • --min-marker-gene-count (int): Factors with fewer marker genes are left Unresolved without an API call (default: 5).
  • --no-specificity (flag): Omit per-gene specificity.
  • --no-sample-markers (flag): Multi-sample: omit per-sample marker genes.

LLM:

  • --model-name (str): LLM model (defaults: claude-opus-5-5 for claude, gpt-5.4-mini for openai, gpt-5-mini for umgpt, gemini-3.5-flash for google).
  • --effort (str): Reasoning effort: low, medium, high, xhigh, max (default: high).
  • --max-factors-per-call (int): Factors per call; 0 sends all factors in one call (default: 0).
  • --max-output-tokens (int): Output budget per call (defaults: 128000 for claude/openai, 64000 for umgpt/google).
  • --threads (int): Parallel LLM calls when there are several (default: 4).
  • --request-timeout (int): Seconds (default: 1800); --max-retries (int): Retries (default: 3).
  • --api-base-url (str): Base URL for openai/umgpt (e.g., a proxy).
  • --no-fallbacks (flag): claude: disable server-side refusal fallbacks.

Run and Report:

  • --dry-run (flag): Write the prompts to <stem>.llm/ and an evidence-only report, without calling the LLM (no TSVs are written).
  • --report-only (flag): Rebuild the report and TSVs from responses saved in <stem>.llm/ without calling the LLM.
  • --no-reuse (flag): Do not reuse responses saved in <stem>.llm/ (they are reused by default).
  • --html (str): Report path (default: <stem>.html); --no-html (flag) skips the report.
  • --dotplot-genes (str): Genes embedded in the report's dotplots: markers (default) or all (larger file).
  • --title (str): Report title (default: dataset and prefix name).
  • --verbose (flag): Verbose logging.

docs.title: Output
docs.text:
With the default stem <prefix>-alias-ai:

  • <stem>.tsv: Alias TSV (index, alias); duplicate aliases get _1, _2, … suffixes and unresolved factors are Unresolved.
  • <stem>.annotations.tsv: One row per factor with status (assigned, ambiguous, unfitted), alias, label, kind, compartment, confidence, key genes, alternatives, rationale, and evidence columns.
  • <stem>.html: Self-contained report with an overview, the factor table, interactive dotplots, and run details.
  • <stem>.llm/: Requests and responses of every LLM call (reused on re-runs unless --no-reuse).
  • <stem>.candidates.json: The merged candidate list (with --candidates auto).

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Features (typically genes) can be filtered at several points of the pipeline. Most commands take the same four flags — --include-feature-list, --exclude-feature-list, --include-feature-regex, --exclude-feature-regex — but what they affect depends on the command:

Command Filter flags What is filtered sge_convert lists and regexes The transcript TSV at ingest, so everything downstream reformat_cosmx lists and regexes The CosMx transcript TSV at ingest run_ficture2 regexes; --in-feature-ficture The LDA model only (the tiled data keep every feature) run_ficture2_multi lists and regexes The LDA training/projection only, via feature_select run_ficture2_multi_cells lists and regexes The per-cell count matrices, so the whole cell analysis feature_filtering lists, substrings, regexes, types Rows of any CSV/TSV with a feature column (standalone) feature_select lists and regexes Writes one resolved feature list

Usually run for you

run_together passes its ingest filters to sge_convert/reformat_cosmx and its analysis filters to run_ficture2_multi, which calls feature_select (see Feature filtering: two independent layers). This page is for running the filters directly in step-by-step or custom workflows; feature_filtering is a standalone add-on that run_together does not call.

docs.title: Regex semantics differ between commands
docs.text:
• Substring (search): sge_convert, reformat_cosmx, run_ficture2_multi, run_ficture2_multi_cells, feature_filtering, and feature_select. A pattern matches if it occurs anywhere in the name; anchor it with ^/$ as needed (e.g. '^mt-').
  • Whole name: run_ficture2, which hands the regexes to punkst lda4hex (std::regex_match). The pattern must match the entire name, e.g. '^(mt-.*|Gm[0-9]+)$' rather than '^(mt-|Gm[0-9])'.

docs.title: Filtering a feature table (feature_filtering)
docs.text: feature_filtering filters the rows of a CSV/TSV (e.g., feature.clean.tsv.gz) by feature name, using explicit lists, substrings, regex patterns, or a feature-type reference file. The filtered file can then be used downstream, for example as run_ficture2 --in-feature-ficture.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Input CSV/TSV with a header line and a feature-name column (plain text or gzipped).
  • A reference file of feature types when using --include-feature-type-regex.

docs.title: Actions
docs.text:
Action Specifications

No action runs by default. Activate at least one filter criterion via the filter parameters.

  • Include criteria are restrictive (a feature must satisfy all provided include constraints).
  • Exclude criteria are subtractive (a feature matching any exclude constraint is removed).

docs.title: 1) Filter by Regex
docs.text:
This example demonstrates an exclude-only pattern with --exclude-feature-regex; conversely, you could keep only matching features using --include-feature-regex.

cartloader feature_filtering \
  --in-csv /path/to/sge/feature.clean.tsv.gz \
  --out-csv /path/to/sge/feature.filtered.tsv.gz \
  --exclude-feature-regex '^(BLANK|NegCon|NegPrb)'

docs.title: 2) Filter by Lists
docs.text:
Include-only and exclude-only lists can be used alone or together. Below is an example using --include-feature-list.

include_list=/path/to/input_keep_genes.txt
cartloader feature_filtering \
  --in-csv /path/to/sge/feature.clean.tsv.gz \
  --out-csv /path/to/sge/feature.filtered.tsv.gz \
  --out-record /path/to/sge/feature.filter_record.tsv \
  --csv-colname-feature-name gene \
  --include-feature-list ${include_list} \
  --log

docs.title: 3) Filter by Substrings
docs.text:
Below, include and exclude are shown together for illustration; you may use either one independently.

cartloader feature_filtering \
  --in-csv /path/to/sge/feature.clean.tsv.gz \
  --out-csv /path/to/sge/feature.neuronal.tsv.gz \
  --include-feature-substr Neur \
  --exclude-feature-substr Pseudo

docs.title: 4) Filter by Feature Types
docs.text:
These examples keep features of a given type using a reference file; adapt the regex to the types you want to keep.

# Example 4A includes `protein_coding` features, selecting columns by name in a TSV reference file.

ref_tsv=/path/to/refs/feature_types.tsv

cartloader feature_filtering \
  --in-csv /path/to/sge/feature.clean.tsv.gz \
  --out-csv /path/to/sge/feature.protein_coding.tsv.gz \
  --include-feature-type-regex '^protein_coding$' \
  --feature-type-ref ${ref_tsv} \
  --feature-type-ref-colname-name gene \
  --feature-type-ref-colname-type type

# Example 4B includes `lncRNA` features, selecting columns by 0-based index in a CSV reference file:

ref_csv=/path/to/refs/gene_types.csv

cartloader feature_filtering \
  --in-csv /path/to/sge/feature.clean.tsv.gz \
  --out-csv /path/to/sge/feature.lncRNA.tsv.gz \
  --include-feature-type-regex '^lncRNA$' \
  --feature-type-ref ${ref_csv} \
  --feature-type-ref-delim "," \
  --feature-type-ref-colidx-name 0 \
  --feature-type-ref-colidx-type 2

docs.title: Input/Output Parameters
docs.text:
• --in-csv (str, required): Input CSV/TSV with a header line (plain text or gzipped).
  • --out-csv (str, required): Output CSV/TSV of the rows kept, gzipped (.gz is appended if missing).
  • --out-record (str): Optional table with the feature and its filtering reason (empty when kept).
  • --csv-colname-feature-name (str): Feature column name in the input file (default: gene).
  • --csv-delim (str): Delimiter of the input, the output and the record (default: \t).
  • --chunksize (int): Chunk size for streaming reads (default: 50000).
  • --log (flag): Write logs to feature_filtering.log next to the outputs.

docs.title: Filters Parameters
docs.text: Regex and substring filters match anywhere in the name (substring semantics). List files are plain text with one feature name per line (no header).

docs.title: List Filters Parameters
docs.text:
• --include-feature-list (str): Path to a file with feature names to include.
  • --exclude-feature-list (str): Path to a file with feature names to exclude.

docs.title: Substring Filters Parameters
docs.text:
• --include-feature-substr (str): Include features containing the substring.
  • --exclude-feature-substr (str): Exclude features containing the substring.

docs.title: Regex Filters Parameters
docs.text:
• --include-feature-regex (str): Include features matching the regex.
  • --exclude-feature-regex (str): Exclude features matching the regex.

docs.title: Type Filters Parameters
docs.text:
Reference file columns (name vs. index)

The reference file is always read with its first line as the header (lines starting with # are skipped). Select the feature-name and feature-type columns either by header name (--feature-type-ref-colname-*) or by 0-based position (--feature-type-ref-colidx-*).

  • --include-feature-type-regex (str): Include features whose type matches the regex (e.g., ^protein_coding$).
  • --feature-type-ref (str): Reference file with feature name and type columns.
  • --feature-type-ref-delim (str): Delimiter of the reference file (default: \t).
  • --feature-type-ref-colname-name (str): Column name for feature name.
  • --feature-type-ref-colname-type (str): Column name for feature type.
  • --feature-type-ref-colidx-name (int): 0-based column index for feature name.
  • --feature-type-ref-colidx-type (int): 0-based column index for feature type.

docs.title: Output
docs.text: A gzipped CSV/TSV with the rows whose feature passed the filters. If --out-record is set, a table mapping each feature to a filtering reason; empty when a feature is kept.

docs.title: Resolving filters into one list (feature_select)
docs.text:
feature_select resolves include/exclude lists and regexes into a single feature list file. It is used:

  • by run_ficture2_multi, which resolves its four filter flags (--mode include) against multi.union_features.tsv into multi.selected_features.tsv and passes it to lda4hex --features, restricting the factor analysis without altering the tiled transcripts or the feature list that packaging reads;
  • by run_ficture2_multi_cells, to fold a list and a regex of the same polarity into one list before spatula;
  • by hand, for sge_convert on the MEX platforms, where a list and a regex of the same polarity cannot be combined.

docs.title: Example Usage
docs.text:
Fold an include list and an include regex into one list (the include list is the universe):

cartloader feature_select \
  --mode include \
  --include-list /path/to/panel_genes.txt \
  --include-regex '^(Cd|Il)' \
  --out /path/to/selected_genes.txt

Fold an exclude list and an exclude regex into one list of features to drop:

cartloader feature_select \
  --mode exclude \
  --in-features /path/to/all_gene_names.txt \
  --exclude-list /path/to/drop_genes.txt \
  --exclude-regex '^(BLANK|NegCon|NegPrb)' \
  --out /path/to/drop_all.txt

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
• --out (str, required): Path to the output feature list.
  • --mode (include|exclude): include (default) writes the features to keep; exclude writes the features to drop.
  • --in-features (str): The universe of features: a TSV whose first column is the feature name and whose optional second column is a count (e.g., multi.union_features.tsv); lines starting with # are skipped. Required unless --mode include with --include-list, in which case the include list is the universe.
  • --include-list, --exclude-list (str): Files of feature names to include/exclude (one per line; only the first tab-separated column is read).
  • --include-regex, --exclude-regex (str): Regexes of feature names to include/exclude (substring semantics).
  • --allow-empty (flag): Write an empty output instead of failing when no feature survives.

docs.title: Output
docs.text:
• --mode include: the universe features that are in --include-list (if given), not in --exclude-list, match --include-regex (if given), and do not match --exclude-regex, in universe order. When every selected feature has a count in the universe, the file starts with a #feature<TAB>total_count header and carries the counts; otherwise it lists names only.
  • --mode exclude: --exclude-list united with the --in-features entries matching --exclude-regex, one name per line. Include flags are not allowed in this mode, and --exclude-regex requires --in-features.

docs.title: Cell Analysis Import
docs.text:
Usually run for you

run_together calls these importers when a platform's cell-analysis outputs are present (e.g., import_visiumhd_cell for Space Ranger segmentation, import_xenium_cell for per-sample Xenium Ranger clusters in joint runs). This page is for importing cell analyses directly, step by step.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Import platform‑specific cell analysis outputs (cells, boundaries, clusters/DE, UMAP), convert them to web‑ready PMTiles layers, write an asset JSON for run_cartload2 --cell-assets, and optionally register them in an existing catalog.yaml. Two commands are available:

  • import_xenium_cell for 10x Xenium Ranger outputs;
  • import_visiumhd_cell for 10x Visium HD Space Ranger segmented outputs.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Cell analysis outputs from the platform (see per‑platform inputs below).
  • Tools (defaults point to the bundled submodules): tippecanoe, spatula, and punkst (--ficture2, for the factor report of regenerated DE); python3; Rscript on PATH for UMAP plots; parquet-tools for a Xenium cells Parquet.
  • An expression source for the pseudobulk/DE that is regenerated by default (see Pseudobulk and DE).
  • For --update-catalog: an existing catalog.yaml from Asset Packaging.

docs.title: Actions
docs.text:
Action Specifications

No action runs by default. Activate at least one using the action parameters.

docs.title: Cell Conversion Step (--cells)
docs.text: Converts cell centroids into <outprefix>-cells.pmtiles with cell_id, count, and topK (cluster index, ranked by cluster size) attributes. Visium HD centroids are derived from the cell polygons.

docs.title: Cell Boundary Conversion Step (--boundaries)
docs.text: Converts cell polygons into <outprefix>-boundaries.geojson (attributes cell_id, topK) and <outprefix>-boundaries.pmtiles.

docs.title: UMAP Conversion Step (--umap)
docs.text: Converts the UMAP projection into <outprefix>-umap.pmtiles and draws UMAP plots. Xenium skips this step with a warning when the projection file is missing; Visium HD stops with an error.

docs.title: Catalog Update (--update-catalog)
docs.text:
Adds (or replaces, by ID) the cell factor in assets.factors of an existing catalog. Not included in --all.

--all enables --cells, --boundaries, and --umap. Every run also writes <outprefix>_assets.json.

docs.title: Pseudobulk and DE
docs.text:
By default both commands regenerate a cluster pseudobulk matrix and a cluster DE table from expression data, rather than using the platform's DE CSV:

  • Xenium: needs either --pixel (a transcript TSV with cell ID, gene, and count columns) or a cell-feature MEX (--mex-dir, or CELL_FEATURE_MEX in the JSON). Use --skip-redo-diffexp to read the DE CSV instead, and add --skip-redo-pseudobulk to skip the pseudobulk (then no expression source is needed).
  • Visium HD: uses the cell-feature MEX (--mtx-cells / CELL_FEATURE_MEX) and runs with --cells. Either --skip-mex-pseudobulk or --skip-mex-diffexp switches to the DE CSV. Run --boundaries together with --cells (or with a skip flag) so a DE table is written.

docs.title: Example Usage
docs.text:
Two Input Modes

Each command accepts one of two mutually exclusive input modes:

  • JSON mode: pass --in-json (e.g., a manifest from load_xenium_ranger / load_space_ranger; keys are read from its CELLS section when present).
  • Manual mode: pass --in-dir; file locations are relative to it (absolute paths are also accepted for Xenium).
Xenium ExampleVisium HD Example 
# JSON input mode (keys: CELL, BOUNDARY, CLUSTER, DE; optional UMAP_PROJ, CELL_FEATURE_MEX)
cartloader import_xenium_cell \
  --all \
  --outprefix /path/to/out/xeniumranger \
  --in-json /path/to/xenium_ranger_assets.json

# Manual input mode (pseudobulk/DE regenerated from the cell-feature MEX)
cartloader import_xenium_cell \
  --all \
  --outprefix /path/to/out/xeniumranger \
  --in-dir /path/to/xenium_ranger_output \
  --csv-cells cells.csv.gz \
  --csv-boundaries cell_boundaries.csv.gz \
  --csv-clust analysis/clustering/gene_expression_graphclust/clusters.csv \
  --csv-diffexp analysis/diffexp/gene_expression_graphclust/differential_expression.csv \
  --mex-dir cell_feature_matrix

# JSON input mode (keys: CELL_FEATURE_MEX, CELL_GEOJSON, CLUSTER, DE; optional UMAP_PROJ; scale from SGE.SCALE)
cartloader import_visiumhd_cell \
  --cells --boundaries \
  --outprefix /path/to/out/spaceranger \
  --in-json /path/to/space_ranger_assets.json

# Manual input mode (defaults match the Space Ranger layout)
cartloader import_visiumhd_cell \
  --cells --boundaries \
  --outprefix /path/to/out/spaceranger \
  --in-dir /path/to/spaceranger_output \
  --mtx-cells segmented_outputs/filtered_feature_cell_matrix \
  --geojson-cells segmented_outputs/cell_segmentations.geojson \
  --csv-clust segmented_outputs/analysis/clustering/gene_expression_graphclust/clusters.csv \
  --csv-diffexp segmented_outputs/analysis/diffexp/gene_expression_graphclust/differential_expression.csv

docs.title: Action Parameters
docs.text:
• --cells (flag): Import segmented cells and generate PMTiles.
  • --boundaries (flag): Import cell boundaries and generate GeoJSON/PMTiles.
  • --umap (flag): Import the UMAP projection and generate PMTiles.
  • --update-catalog (flag): Update an existing catalog.yaml.
  • --all (flag): Enable --cells, --boundaries, and --umap.

docs.title: Input/Output Parameters
docs.text:
• --outprefix (str, required): Output prefix (e.g., /path/to/out/sample).
  • --id (str): Identifier for the cell factor (default: basename of --outprefix).
  • --name (str): Display name for the cell factor (default: basename of --outprefix).
Xenium InputVisium HD Input

JSON Mode:

  • --in-json (str): JSON/YAML with keys CELL, BOUNDARY, CLUSTER, DE, and optionally UMAP_PROJ, CELL_FEATURE_MEX, PIXEL.

Manual Mode (relative to --in-dir, or absolute):

  • --in-dir (str): Base input directory.
  • --csv-cells (str): Cell table, CSV or Parquet (default: cells.csv.gz).
  • --csv-boundaries (str): Cell boundary CSV whose first three columns are cell ID, X, and Y (default: cell_boundaries.csv.gz).
  • --csv-clust (str): Cluster CSV (default: analysis/clustering/gene_expression_graphclust/clusters.csv).
  • --csv-diffexp (str): DE CSV (default: analysis/diffexp/gene_expression_graphclust/differential_expression.csv).
  • --csv-umap (str): UMAP projection CSV (default: analysis/umap/gene_expression_2_components/projection.csv).
  • --mex-dir (str): Cell-feature MEX directory for pseudobulk/DE (e.g., cell_feature_matrix; default: none).
  • --mex-bcd / --mex-ftr / --mex-mtx (str): MEX file names (default: barcodes.tsv.gz / features.tsv.gz / matrix.mtx.gz).

Expression source and DE:

  • --pixel (str): Transcript TSV with cell IDs, used as given (not under --in-dir); takes precedence over --mex-dir. In JSON mode the path is read from the PIXEL key and --pixel only selects this route.
  • --pixel-colname-cell-id / --pixel-colname-gene / --pixel-colname-count (str): Columns in --pixel (default: cell_id / gene / count).
  • --skip-redo-diffexp (flag): Use the DE CSV instead of regenerating DE.
  • --skip-redo-pseudobulk (flag): Do not regenerate the pseudobulk (requires --skip-redo-diffexp).

JSON Mode:

  • --in-json (str): JSON/YAML with keys CELL_FEATURE_MEX, CELL_GEOJSON, CLUSTER, DE, and optionally UMAP_PROJ (under CELLS); SGE.SCALE supplies the scale JSON.

Manual Mode (relative to --in-dir):

  • --in-dir (str): Space Ranger output directory.
  • --mtx-cells (str): Cell-feature MEX directory (default: segmented_outputs/filtered_feature_cell_matrix).
  • --geojson-cells (str): Cell segmentation GeoJSON (default: segmented_outputs/cell_segmentations.geojson).
  • --csv-clust (str): Cluster CSV (default: segmented_outputs/analysis/clustering/gene_expression_graphclust/clusters.csv).
  • --csv-diffexp (str): DE CSV (default: segmented_outputs/analysis/diffexp/gene_expression_graphclust/differential_expression.csv).
  • --csv-umap (str): UMAP projection CSV (default: segmented_outputs/analysis/umap/gene_expression_2_components/projection.csv).
  • --mex-bcd / --mex-ftr / --mex-mtx (str): MEX file names (default: barcodes.tsv.gz / features.tsv.gz / matrix.mtx.gz).
  • --scale-json (str): Scale factors JSON (default: binned_outputs/square_002um/spatial/scalefactors_json.json). It must exist and sets --units-per-um from microns_per_pixel; pass --scale-json "" to use --units-per-um instead.
  • --units-per-um (float): Coordinate units per µm, used only without a scale JSON (default: 1).

DE:

  • --skip-mex-pseudobulk / --skip-mex-diffexp (flag): Use the DE CSV instead of regenerating pseudobulk/DE from the MEX.
Auxiliary Parameters

PMTiles Conversion:

  • --min-zoom / --max-zoom (int): Zoom range for cells and boundaries (default: 10 / 18).
  • --umap-min-zoom / --umap-max-zoom (int): Zoom range for UMAP (default: 0 / 18).
  • --max-tile-bytes (int): Max bytes per tile (default: 5000000).
  • --max-feature-counts (int): Max features per tile (default: 500000).
  • --preserve-point-density-thres (int): Point density threshold (default: 1024).

Coloring and DE:

  • --tsv-cmap (str): Cluster color table TSV (default: <cartloader_dir>/assets/default_color_map.tsv).
  • --de-max-pval (float): Max p-value (default: 0.01).
  • --de-min-fc (float): Min fold change (default: 1.2).

Catalog:

  • --catalog-yaml (str): Catalog to update (default: catalog.yaml in the directory of --outprefix).
  • --out-catalog-yaml (str): Write the updated catalog here instead of overwriting --catalog-yaml.

Column Names:

Xenium only:

  • --cells-colname-cell-id / --cells-colname-x / --cells-colname-y / --cells-colname-count (default: cell_id / x_centroid / y_centroid / transcript_counts)
  • --boundaries-colname-cell-id / --boundaries-colname-x / --boundaries-colname-y (default: cell_id / vertex_x / vertex_y)

Both:

  • --clust-colname-barcode / --clust-colname-cluster (default: Barcode / Cluster; common aliases such as cell_id or cluster are also recognized)
  • --umap-colname-barcode / --umap-colname-x / --umap-colname-y (default: Barcode / UMAP-1 / UMAP-2)

Run and Environment:

  • --threads (int): Threads for tippecanoe (default: 4).
  • --tmp-dir (str): Temporary directory (default: tmp/ in the directory of --outprefix).
  • --keep-intermediate-files (flag): Keep intermediate files.
  • --log (flag) / --log-suffix (str): Write a log next to the outputs (default suffix: .log).
  • --tippecanoe (str): Default <cartloader_dir>/submodules/tippecanoe/tippecanoe.
  • --spatula (str): Default <cartloader_dir>/submodules/spatula/bin/spatula.
  • --ficture2 (str): punkst repository (default: <cartloader_dir>/submodules/punkst).
  • --python, --gzip, --sort (str): Binaries on PATH (default: python3, gzip, sort).
  • --R (str): Checked before UMAP plotting (default: Rscript for Xenium, R for Visium HD); the plots themselves call Rscript.
  • --parquet-tools (str): Xenium only; for a Parquet --csv-cells (default: parquet-tools).

docs.title: Output
docs.text:
Written next to --outprefix:

  • <outprefix>-cells.pmtiles and <outprefix>-cells.csv: Cell centroids with cell_id, count, topK.
  • <outprefix>-boundaries.pmtiles and <outprefix>-boundaries.geojson: Cell polygons with cell_id, topK.
  • <outprefix>-rgb.tsv: Cluster color table.
  • <outprefix>-cells-bulk-de.tsv: Cluster DE table.
  • <outprefix>-pseudobulk.tsv.gz and <outprefix>-info.tsv: Cluster pseudobulk and factor info (when regenerated).
  • <outprefix>-umap.tsv.gz, <outprefix>-umap.pmtiles, <outprefix>.umap.png, <outprefix>.umap.single.binary.png: UMAP outputs (with --umap).
  • <outprefix>_assets.json: Cell asset entry for run_cartload2 --cell-assets (always written).
  • With --update-catalog: the catalog rewritten with the cell factor in assets.factors.

docs.title: Background Image Import
docs.text:
Usually run for you

run_together calls import_image in its images stage for each image modality you declare (see Image Modalities). This page is for importing an image directly, step by step.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
import_image loads a histology or background image (OME‑TIFF, TIFF, or PNG) and produces a georeferenced, web‑ready raster PMTiles layer, with optional orientation transforms and catalog registration.

Question

  • How do I decide orientation for background image import?

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Input image: OME‑TIFF, TIFF, or PNG.
  • A bounds source unless the image already carries a geotransform: OME metadata (--ome2png or --georef-detect ome), or explicit bounds (--georef-bounds, --georef-bounds-tsv, --georef-pixel-tsv).
  • Tools: geotiff2pmtiles (default: bundled submodule), and GDAL's gdalwarp, gdalinfo, and gdal_translate on PATH (gdal_translate is needed for georeferencing).
  • For --update-catalog: an existing catalog.yaml (e.g., from run_cartload2).

docs.title: Actions
docs.text:
Action Specifications

No action runs by default. Pass at least one of --ome2png, --png2pmtiles, --georeference, --rotate, --flip-vertical, or --flip-horizontal. Georeferencing and orientation are applied inside the PNG‑to‑PMTiles step, so they take effect only together with --png2pmtiles.

docs.title: OME‑TIFF to PNG Step (--ome2png)
docs.text: Extracts a PNG from an OME‑TIFF (cartloader image_ome2png), reads its bounds from the OME metadata (or from --micron2pixel-csv / --px-per-um-x/y), and records its color mode. This also turns on --georeference with those bounds, so --georef-bounds, --georef-bounds-tsv, and --georef-pixel-tsv cannot be combined with it.

docs.title: Georeference Step (--georeference)
docs.text: Assigns bounds and the spatial reference (--srs) to the image with gdal_translate. Provide exactly one bounds source: --georef-bounds, --georef-bounds-tsv, --georef-pixel-tsv, or --georef-detect (ome or gtiff).

docs.title: Orientation Step (--rotate, --flip-vertical, --flip-horizontal)
docs.text: Rotates the georeferenced image clockwise by 90/180/270 degrees and/or flips it (rotation before flips) with gdalwarp. Equivalent combinations are normalized first (e.g., --rotate 180 becomes both flips).

docs.title: PNG to PMTiles Step (--png2pmtiles)
docs.text: Converts the (georeferenced, oriented) image into <img-id>.pmtiles with geotiff2pmtiles and writes <img-id>_assets.json. The image must carry a coordinate system at this point; otherwise the step stops with an error rather than writing an empty layer.

docs.title: Catalog Update Step (--update-catalog)
docs.text: Adds <img-id>.pmtiles to the catalog as a basemap with ID <img-id>. The catalog (--catalog-yaml, default <out-dir>/catalog.yaml) must already exist; otherwise the run stops because make finds no rule for it.

docs.title: 1) OME‑TIFF → PNG → PMTiles (auto georeference)
docs.text:
IMAGE_ID=TEST_ID      # replace TEST_ID with your own ID (no whitespace)

cartloader import_image \
  --ome2png --png2pmtiles --update-catalog \
  --in-img /path/to/input.ome.tif \
  --out-dir /path/to/out \
  --img-id  ${IMAGE_ID}

docs.title: 2) PNG → PMTiles (manual georeference via bounds)
docs.text:
Pick one bounds input method and enable --georeference.

IMAGE_ID=TEST_ID      # replace TEST_ID with your own ID (no whitespace)

# A) Bounds string
cartloader import_image \
  --png2pmtiles --georeference \
  --in-img /path/to/image.png \
  --georef-bounds "ulx,uly,lrx,lry" \
  --out-dir /path/to/out \
  --img-id ${IMAGE_ID}

# B) Bounds TSV
cartloader import_image \
  --png2pmtiles --georeference \
  --in-img /path/to/image.png \
  --georef-bounds-tsv /path/to/bounds.tsv \
  --out-dir /path/to/out \
  --img-id ${IMAGE_ID}

# C) OME-TIFF metadata (e.g., an 8-bit RGB H&E OME-TIFF), without extracting a PNG first
cartloader import_image \
